Zambia’s 2021 Floods: Economic Impact and Recovery One Year On

LUSAKA—One year after severe flooding inundated much of Zambia, the country’s economy has largely stabilized, though the effects of the natural disaster are still keenly felt across multiple sectors. The floods, which struck in January and February 2021 following unprecedented rainfall, disrupted supply chains, damaged infrastructure, and forced temporary shutdowns at major industrial operations including the Chambishi Copper Smelter Ltd.

According to the Zambia Meteorological Department, rainfall during the 2020/2021 wet season was 30% above the long-term average, with the Northern, Copperbelt, and Central provinces hardest hit. The flooding displaced over 100,000 people, destroyed thousands of hectares of farmland, and led to the temporary closure of key transportation routes, including sections of the Great North Road.

For the mining industry—Zambia’s economic backbone—the floods posed significant challenges. Chambishi Copper Smelter Ltd was among the operators forced to halt production for several days due to waterlogged access roads and power outages. “The safety of our workforce was our top priority,” said a company spokesperson. “Operations resumed only after thorough inspections and repairs to affected facilities.”

Trade data from the Zambia Chamber of Mines indicates copper exports dipped by 4% in the first quarter of 2021 compared to the previous year, with analysts attributing much of the decline to disrupted logistics. Other sectors, such as agriculture and retail, also reported losses. The Zambia National Farmers’ Union estimated crop damage at over ZMW 300 million, particularly in maize and soya bean yields.

Efforts to restore normalcy have included government investment in road repairs, expanded drainage systems, and targeted support for affected communities. “We have worked closely with the private sector to ensure that infrastructure is rebuilt to withstand future events,” said Infrastructure Minister Charles Lusambo. “Our focus is on resilience and preparedness.”

While the immediate disruptions have passed, economists note that the 2021 floods exposed vulnerabilities in Zambia’s transport and energy networks. “The episode was a wake-up call for the country,” said Lusaka-based economist Felicia Chanda. “Greater investment in climate adaptation and risk mitigation is essential for long-term growth.”

With the mining industry, including Chambishi Copper Smelter Ltd, now operating at full capacity, Zambia’s economy is projected to recover fully by the end of 2022. However, the memory of the 2021 floods continues to shape the national conversation on disaster preparedness and sustainable development.
